title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: the subject decides, and the d disappears

questions.prompt: A pupil must join these two facts into one sentence of purpose: "The nurse writes everything down." and "The doctor can read the file quickly." Which version is correct?

options.text: The nurse writes everything down to the doctor read the file quickly.
The nurse writes everything down so that the doctor can read the file quickly.
The nurse writes everything down in order to the doctor read the file quickly.
The nurse writes everything down for the doctor to reading the file quickly.

questions.explanation: Two different people act here — the nurse writes, the doctor reads — so the purpose must be carried by a full clause, and that is what so that introduces, with can among the eight modals the grammar box allows after it. to plus a verb is reserved for sentences whose two halves share one subject, which is why the first version collapses as soon as the doctor appears. in order to is the same structure in a more formal dress and fails for the same reason. And the last version at least sees that the doctor must be named, but it puts an -ing form after to, where English wants the base verb.

questions.prompt: Which of these four sentences is written correctly?

options.text: Did your grandmother used to live in Sfax?
Your grandmother didn't used to live in Sfax.
Your grandmother use to live in Sfax.
Your grandmother used to live in Sfax.

questions.explanation: In the affirmative the form keeps its d: used to plus the base verb, which is what the last sentence writes. The first two both put did or didn't in front and then keep the d as well, which doubles the past — after did every verb returns to its base form, so the correct versions are did your grandmother use to live and didn't use to live. The third makes the opposite mistake: it drops the d in a sentence that has no did to carry it, leaving the past unmarked anywhere. Between the four, only one places the d exactly where the sentence needs it.

questions.prompt: Read this note from a hospital corridor: "He looks pale. He must have skipped lunch again." and this one: "He should have eaten before the operation." What separates them?

options.text: The first concludes from evidence, the second regrets an omission.
The first states an obligation, the second grants a permission to leave.
The first is about the future, the second about the past.
The first is certain, the second is a question.

questions.explanation: The pale face is the evidence, and must have plus a past participle states the conclusion the writer draws from it; should have plus a past participle names something that ought to have happened and did not, which is regret. Neither is an obligation or a permission: must can oblige when it stands alone with a base verb, but followed by have and a participle it measures how sure the speaker is. Both look backwards, so no reading that puts one of them in the future can hold. And neither is a question, since both end in a full stop and keep the ordinary word order of a statement.

questions.prompt: A pupil sorts eight words by the sound of their final -s and puts them in three columns. Which word is in the wrong column?

options.text: /s/ — check-ups
/z/ — goes
/ɪz/ — wishes
/s/ — affairs

questions.explanation: affairs ends in the voiced r, where the throat vibrates, so the ending is /z/ and not /s/ — that single test settles every word in the exercise. check-ups ends in the voiceless p, where nothing vibrates, so /s/ is right. goes ends in a vowel sound, which is voiced like every vowel, so /z/ is right there too. And wishes puts the hiss of sh immediately before the ending, which is the one case where English has to insert a vowel and produce /ɪz/. Three of the four are correctly placed; only the one after the r is not.

questions.prompt: Emma's story gives three ages: eleven, thirty, thirty-six. Which pairing is right?

options.text: At eleven she set up her company; at thirty she won a scholarship.
At eleven she won a scholarship; at thirty she set up her company.
At thirty she began piano lessons; at thirty-six she won a scholarship.
At eleven she employed thirty teachers; at thirty-six she began teaching.

questions.explanation: The text places the scholarship to music school at eleven and the founding of The Music House for Children at thirty, after a children's concert she helped a friend organise. Reversing the two would have a child of eleven running a business and a woman of thirty starting music school, which the story contradicts twice over. Her piano lessons belong to early childhood, before the scholarship, so nothing about them can sit at thirty. And thirty is the number of teachers she employs at thirty-six, not an age at which anything was founded — the lesson puts the two thirties close together on purpose.

questions.prompt: Your book asks you to fill this gap: "Each animal often ……… as much as four hundred pounds, and it could ……… twenty miles a day." Which pair is right?

options.text: used to carry … used to travel
carried … to travel
carried … travel
was carrying … travelling

questions.explanation: The first gap already has often in front of it, so the repetition is stated and a plain past simple is enough — carried. The second gap follows could, and a modal is always followed by the base verb with nothing between, which gives travel. Adding used to in the first half repeats what often has just said, and putting it after could is impossible in any case, since two modal-like forms cannot stack. Keeping to after could breaks the same rule from the other side. And a past progressive would turn a habit that lasted centuries into one long action in progress, which is not what a caravan of camels does.
